title: The Price of the Mountain Mint
subtitle: The Lanternweald — expansion pass three
content:
The supplier's letter smelled of rain and spoiled leaves.

Iroh read it at the back counter, his expression growing more serious with every line.

"Bad news?" I asked.

"The mountain harvest was poor. Too much rain at the wrong time."

He handed me the note.

The supplier had lost nearly half the expected mint crop. Transporting what remained would cost more, and the farmers had asked their regular buyers to take smaller orders rather than forcing prices low enough to leave families without income.

"They're trying to share the loss," I said.

"Yes."

"Can we manage with less?"

Iroh looked toward the tea tins.

"We can. But not if I insist on serving everything as though nothing has changed."

He sounded unhappy about it.

The Jasmine Dragon had already lost stock in the roof leak. We needed another shipment, but the price was now nearly twice what we'd planned. The bakery was feeling the same shortage in some of its herbs. At the clinic, Katara's volunteers had been rationing mint for certain medicinal preparations.

None of this could be solved by wishing a more generous harvest into existence.

We called a meeting with the people who relied on the shipments.

Mara arrived with flour on her sleeve. Tamsin brought a pencil and the expression of somebody prepared to object to numbers that didn't add up. Neri came with the route schedule. Aang had sent a note from Riverstone asking us to prioritize the clinic's confirmed medicinal needs.

Iroh poured a simpler tea than usual.

Nobody complained.

"We can divide what remains," he said, "but I will not ask the growers to sell at a loss."

Mara nodded.

"Good. They're people, not a cupboard."

Mina turned the supplier's note over and ruled three columns on the back: what had been ordered, what could be spared, and what somebody had actually promised to pay for.

"Before you negotiate," she said, "tell us whose money is being used."

"Mine, if we must cover the shortfall," Iroh replied.

"Your share of the business, you mean. The apprentices' wages aren't a reserve fund."

He inclined his head. "You are correct."

Tamsin checked the proposed carriage route against the rain damage. One road was quicker, but the wheels would cut through an untested embankment. Neri pointed to the longer road and said the carriers had asked for proper rest stops along it.

"We can ask the grower to split the shipment," Iroh said, drawing arrows across the margin. "One sealed crate for the clinic, smaller tins for the other buyers. Nothing moves until the carrier confirms the price."

Mara frowned at the page. "That will mean less mint in my bread."

"Yes," Iroh said. "And I shall have less in my finest tea."

"You're taking that very bravely."

"With considerable suffering."

I laughed. The humor did not make the shortage smaller; it kept us from treating it as an opportunity to praise ourselves. The decision was still going to cost money and disappoint customers. Iroh counted the crates a second time rather than insisting that good intentions would somehow fit more leaves inside them.

The figures were less encouraging.

The clinic needed a guaranteed supply. The bakery could change two recipes. The teahouse could reduce its premium blend, but enough customers depended on the ordinary tea for a small comfort during their working day that raising every price would hurt people who had little to spare.

"Then don't raise every price," I said.

Tamsin lifted an eyebrow.

"Where does the money come from?"

"Let's find out before we guess."

We listed the costs on one sheet: tea, fuel, clean water, staff time, transport, cup repairs, and an emergency reserve. Iroh watched me write.

"You're forgetting something," he said.

"What?"

"Payment for the growers' risk."

I added it.

The numbers became uglier.

Mara smiled.

"At least they're honest."

A good part of the morning went into arguing over what fair meant. Iroh wanted everyone to have the best tea he could serve. Tamsin wanted the business to survive. Neri wanted the delivery route kept open. I wanted us to stop talking as though these desires were enemies.

In the end, we designed three offerings.

The ordinary house blend would remain affordable. It used local herbs and roasted grain with a little citrus peel, warm and pleasant without pretending to be rare mountain mint. A smaller premium service would cost more and use the limited mint supply, with the price clearly explained. The clinic's confirmed allotment would be reserved before any tea was sold.

"No free miracle," I said.

"No," Iroh agreed. "Just careful work."

We posted the menu that afternoon.

The first customer read it, frowned, and asked why the famous mountain mint tea had become so expensive.

Iroh explained the harvest without turning the farmers into a tragedy for entertainment.

"Then what is that one?" the customer asked, pointing to the house blend.

"A new recipe," Iroh said. "It may disappoint you."

The customer sniffed the cup.

"Smells good."

"It is intended to."

They tasted it.

"Hm."

I waited.

"I'll have another."

Iroh's eyebrows rose.

We both tried not to look relieved.

The second customer complained that a famous shop shouldn't serve a cheaper alternative. The third asked if the house blend came in a travel flask. By evening, we'd sold more of it than we'd expected.

Not everyone was pleased. That was normal. A business could make a fair decision and still disappoint someone.

The dispute wasn't over the price of mint. It was over a single line on the supplier's receipt: *Carriage cost to be absorbed by buyer.*

“What does that mean?” Mara asked.

“It means the merchant wants us to pay the additional cart fee,” Iroh said.

“And if we don't?”

“Then the growers may have to.”

Mina took the invoice from him. “Or the merchant is charging us the old fee plus a second one and hoping no one asks.”

For a moment Iroh looked offended on behalf of the whole system of trade. Then he smiled without much pleasure.

“That,” he said, “is why I prefer a good ledger to a convincing speech.”

We sent a message asking the growers to confirm what they had agreed to and to whom they had already paid. The answer came back by evening: the carrier had raised his fee once, not twice. The extra line was an error made by a new clerk in the warehouse. We could settle the genuine cost without taking it out of anyone's harvest.

“Easy fix,” I said.

“It is easy only because Mina questioned it,” Iroh replied.

She was checking the sealed tins for damp leaves. “And because the farmers answered. Don't leave them out.”

He inclined his head. “Nor shall I.”

The next menu draft listed the actual shortage and price. It did not tell a story about a heroic shopkeeper saving a village. The growers had done their work. We were trying to do ours.

Mina brought the day's receipts over and helped us compare the cost of the new house blend with the old mountain mint. She'd been fielding customer complaints since morning and had a better idea than either of us about which substitutions people actually liked.

"We should write the reason for the change on the menu," she said. "Not a sad story about the mountain. Just the supply shortage and the new price."

Iroh nodded. "And the growers should be paid what they asked."

"Yes. That should be in the ledger, not in the speech you plan to make."

He looked wounded. I laughed into my sleeve.

We calculated what it would cost to keep one small tin of the rarer mint for customers who specifically wanted it. The rest of the menu could use local herbs whose sources had been checked. No one suggested sneaking unverified plants into a blend to make it seem luxurious.

Iroh wrote the numbers neatly, then looked up at me.

"Do you mind that our next evening won't be quite so extravagant?"

"What did you plan?"

"Tea. A walk. Possibly two sweet buns."

"That's a terrible disappointment."

His smile brightened. "Two very good sweet buns."

I reached across the counter to touch his hand. We had spoken openly about how I preferred polyamory and practiced ethical non-monogamy. A chosen evening together didn't become less intimate because I could love other people, or because the expensive mint had become scarce.

"Then I would like your company more than the rare tea," I said.

"An excellent investment."

He leaned close and waited. I kissed him briefly, then we returned to the till before Mina could accuse us of holding up the accounts. There were growers to pay and tomorrow's menu to prepare. This particular romance came with receipts.

After closing, I helped Iroh count the till. He checked each coin twice, separated payment owed to workers from money needed for stock, and put a small sum in the repair reserve.

"You're quiet," I said.

He looked up.

"I was remembering an old habit."

"Which one?"

"Thinking generosity meant giving something beautiful without asking what it cost."

I leaned against the counter.

"And now?"

"Now I think generosity sometimes means saying the price aloud and making sure the people who grow the tea can eat."

I smiled.

"That sounds like a lesson worth keeping."

He closed the ledger.

"Would you like to taste the final blend? I changed the citrus balance."

"Is that an invitation or a request for a quality-control volunteer?"

"Both. I am very efficient."

We brewed the last test cup together.

It tasted of toasted grain, orange peel, and a touch of wild rosemary. It was not the expensive tea. It was good on its own terms.

"I like it," I said.

"You needn't be kind."

"I'm not."

He smiled.

Then he pulled a small paper packet from his sleeve.

"One thing the supplier included."

Inside was a handful of dried mountain mint, no more than enough for a private pot.

"They sent a gift?"

"A thank-you for accepting the reduced order."

I touched the edge of the packet.

"Are you going to save it for someone important?"

"I had thought of sharing it with someone important."

I met his eyes.

He lifted my hand and kissed it, then looked suddenly shy in a way that still surprised me after all our time together.

"Tomorrow evening?" he asked.

"I would love that."

He tucked the packet away again. We walked home past the lanterns, with the new menu posted and the accounts balanced as far as they could be balanced.

The next day, a farmer from the supplier's district sent a brief note thanking the teahouse for paying the agreed price. It wasn't a blessing from the spirits or a sudden end to the shortage.

It was proof that someone on the other side of the road had been treated fairly.

Iroh placed the note beside the ledger.

When the kettle boiled that evening, he opened the small packet.

We shared the mint without pretending it had cost nothing.
